question: Which part of the neuron receives incoming signals from other cells?
explanation: Dendrites are the branched extensions of a neuron that act like antennae to pick up chemical and electrical messages from neighboring cells. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h1)

question: What is the main job of the myelin sheath along an axon?

options.A: To connect the dendrites directly to the cell nucleus
options.B: To insulate the fiber and speed up electrical impulse travel
options.C: To manufacture neurotransmitters for chemical synapses
options.D: To anchor the neuron firmly within muscle tissue

explanation: Myelin acts as an insulation layer around the nerve fiber, preventing signal loss and helping electrical impulses travel much faster. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h1)

question: What is the typical electrical charge inside a resting neuron?
explanation: When a neuron is at rest, its internal charge sits at about -70 mV, making the inside more negative than the outside. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h2)

question: How do sodium-potassium pumps maintain the resting charge of a cell?

options.A: By pumping sodium out and potassium into the cell using energy
options.B: By balancing calcium and chloride ions without using energy
options.C: By destroying excess potassium ions inside the cytoplasm
options.D: By allowing sodium to flood inward freely through open gates

explanation: The sodium-potassium pump uses cellular energy to continuously push three sodium ions out and pull two potassium ions in to keep the resting state stable. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h2)

question: Which ion rushes into the neuron when an impulse first starts?
explanation: When a nerve signal starts, special channels open up and allow sodium ions to rush inside, changing the cell charge from negative to positive. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h3)

question: What happens if a stimulus is too weak to reach the threshold of -55 mV?

options.A: A very slow action potential travels down the axon
options.B: No action potential will be generated at all
options.C: The cell permanently loses its resting potential
options.D: Only potassium channels open to create a small spike

explanation: Nerve signals follow an all-or-none rule. If the stimulus does not reach the -55 mV threshold, the neuron simply does not fire. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h3)

question: Why does the absolute refractory period prevent a second nerve impulse right away?

options.A: The myelin sheath has melted away completely
options.B: Potassium pumps have stopped working permanently
options.C: The cell has run out of all water molecules

explanation: During the absolute refractory period, the sodium channels take a brief break and enter an inactive state where they cannot open again immediately. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h4)

question: What is the main purpose of the refractory period in nerve transmission?

options.A: Producing extra neurotransmitters for the next cell
options.B: Speeding up the movement of ions across the axon
options.C: Ensuring impulses travel in only one direction
options.D: Keeping the resting membrane potential permanently positive

explanation: By making the recently fired part of the axon temporarily unresponsive, the refractory period ensures the nerve signal moves forward and does not double back. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h4)

question: What are the tiny gaps in the myelin sheath where nerve signals actually occur called?
explanation: The exposed spaces between segments of the myelin sheath are called nodes of Ranvier, and they contain high concentrations of ion channels. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h5)

question: How does saltatory conduction affect the speed of a nerve impulse?

options.A: It slows down the signal so the brain can process it clearly
options.B: It makes the impulse travel much faster by jumping between nodes
options.C: It converts the electrical signal into a purely chemical hormone
options.D: It stops the signal entirely until energy is replenished

explanation: Saltatory conduction lets the electrical signal leap quickly from one node of Ranvier to the next, speeding up transmission significantly. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h5)

question: What is the tiny space between two communicating neurons called?
explanation: The synaptic cleft is the microscopic gap between the end of one neuron and the start of the next cell. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h6)

question: What role does calcium play when a nerve impulse reaches the end of an axon?

options.A: It triggers vesicles to release neurotransmitters into the cleft
options.B: It destroys excess myelin to allow direct cell contact
options.C: It converts the nerve cell into a muscular fiber
options.D: It immediately stops all electrical activity in the neuron

explanation: When calcium enters the end of the axon, it causes tiny storage sacs to release chemical messengers into the synaptic space. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h6)

question: How do local anesthetics like lidocaine help relieve pain during an episiotomy repair?

options.A: By increasing the resting potential to make firing easier
options.B: By dissolving the myelin sheath surrounding motor neurons
options.C: By blocking voltage-gated sodium channels to stop pain signals
options.D: By destroying neurotransmitters inside the spinal cord

explanation: Lidocaine stops pain by blocking sodium channels, which prevents nerve cells from firing and sending pain signals to the brain. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT related to nerve physiology in obstetric care?

options.A: Using magnesium sulfate to calm central nervous system irritability in eclampsia
options.B: Calculating the exact daily caloric intake required for fetal bone growth
options.C: Applying local anesthetics for pain relief during perineal tear repair
options.D: Administering epidural anesthesia to block pain pathways during labor

explanation: Caloric intake and fetal bone development deal with nutrition and growth, not nerve signal transmission. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h7)
